mappings.note: Dates the Gupta empire to the 3rd-6th centuries CE. Chronology under the goal; no LO covers dating.
Defines 'codified' as systematically arranged in writing, in the context of Ayurvedic texts. Textual history, so the goal.
The shift from post-Kushana regional powers to Gupta consolidation. A political-development narrative rather than a measure of administration.
Recall that Chandragupta II bore the title Vikramaditya. Asked as a name, unlike the maharajadhiraja and chakravartin items, which analyse titles as claims to supremacy and carry LO-124.
Samudragupta as a veena player on his coins and in the prashasti. Cultural history inferred from sources.
Identifies Aryabhata from a correct explanation of lunar eclipses. Scientific history under the goal.
Matches Gupta-era figures to their domains and rejects Varahamihira as a dramatist. Intellectual history.
Accepts the Gupta mathematical advances but rejects the claim that they did not travel abroad. A judgement about the transmission of knowledge, so the goal.
Statements on Kalidasa, Aryabhata's pi and the Charaka Samhita's true subject. Mixed intellectual-history recall.

Vishnu as the deity the Gupta rulers followed, with Garuda in their iconography. A fact about religious affiliation read from coins and inscriptions; the items that analyse tolerance as a policy carry LO-124 instead.
Defines 'outcastes' as those excluded from the social order, as Faxian described the chandalas. Social history; the civics equality outcomes concern the Constitution and the present day.
Kanchipuram as the Pallava capital. A place recall; the item on its thousand temples carries LO-126 because it concerns temple building.
Rulers founding and supporting ghatikas is read as a state commitment to education - a measure adopted by a kingdom. Distinguished from the earlier item that merely defines what a ghatika was.

Samudragupta defeating distant rulers but leaving them in place as tributaries is a consistent method of control. Not LO-125, because it is one ruler's approach applied twice, not two rulers compared.
Matches Gupta-period texts to their subjects, keyed on the Sushruta Samhita. Textual history under the goal.
Modern state support for research and the arts likened to Gupta patronage. A period-characterisation analogy, so the goal.
Rejects the Delhi Sultanate as a Gupta contemporary since it belongs to a much later period. Chronological placement.
Iron as the material of the Delhi pillar. Technological history; LO-126 is about temples, tombs and mosques.
'Dharani-bandha' as the ambition to bind the earth under one sovereignty. Imperial aim, the same reading as its companion item.
Faxian's account of chandalas segregated outside the city set against his picture of prosperity. Social history and source criticism together.
Names the Sushruta Samhita alongside the Charaka Samhita. Textual history under the goal.

Pallava structural temples and rock-cut caves read as patronage of architecture and religious expression - exactly the temple style and technology outcome. Not CG-SST2, because the answer rests on what they built.
A widowed princess ruling as regent and holding the alliance with her father's empire has to be identified as Prabhavati Gupta. Governance and diplomacy, so LO-124.
Matches regions to their ruling dynasties and rejects the Kushanas in Tamil Nadu. Historical geography.
Rejects the claim that Sanskrit literature declined and keeps Kalidasa in the Gupta era. Literary history under the goal.
Statements on Gupta trade with the Mediterranean, the Huna invasions and the false claim that the Pallava kingdom was annexed. Mixed period recall, so the goal rather than LO-124.
Nalanda as the Buddhist university patronised in this period. Educational and institutional history; the item asks which centre, not how it was governed.
Defines Prakrit as the spoken vernaculars beside classical Sanskrit. Linguistic and source history.
Accepts Aryabhata's rotating Earth but rejects the claim of immediate universal acceptance. A judgement about how scientific ideas spread, so the goal.
Names the Iron Pillar at Mehrauli. A monument recall about metallurgy, not about temple construction.
Analyses land grants as decentralised governance securing revenue and loyalty, with copper plates giving permanence. The clearest administrative-measure item in the chapter.
Trade funding patronage and carrying ideas into the Gupta age. Economic and cultural history; no LO covers commerce.
Links political stability and patronage to the flourishing of science, letters and art. A judgement about the conditions of a cultural age.
Compares Aryabhata's theoretical astronomy with Varahamihira's encyclopedic applied science. Intellectual history; LO-125 compares rulers' policies, not scholars.
Evaluates Vaishnava rulers who nonetheless funded Nalanda and other traditions - a policy of the state towards religious communities. Not LO-127, because no new movement is emerging.

Characterises Gupta art and architecture, including the Sarnath Buddha, Ajanta and the first structural temples such as Deogarh. The temple-development strand puts it under LO-126 rather than the general goal.

Contrasts northern fragmentation under Huna pressure with Pallava consolidation in the south. A regional comparison of political trajectories; LO-125 would need two rulers' policies set against each other.
Kanchipuram's 'thousand temples' explained by sustained Pallava temple-building patronage. Temple construction, so LO-126; the item naming it as their capital stays with the goal.
Kalidasa as the author of Meghadutam. Literary recall under the goal.
Ayurveda as the medical system codified in the Gupta era. Textual and scientific history.
